title: 2 Kings 14:1–14
context: Amaziah son of Joash reigns over Judah. He does what is right, yet not like David, and the high places remain. He punishes his father’s murderers but spares their children according to the law of Moses, then defeats Edom. Flush with victory, he challenges Jehoash of Israel, who answers with a parable of a thistle and a cedar. Amaziah refuses to listen, is defeated and captured at Beth Shemesh, and Jerusalem’s wall is broken down and its treasures taken. A cubit is about 18 inches or 46 centimeters, so the four-hundred-cubit breach is roughly 600 feet. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about pride and mixed obedience.

verses.text: In the second year of Joash, son of Joahaz, king of Israel, Amaziah the son of Joash king of Judah began to reign.
verses.arminianNotes:
Amaziah son of Joash begins to reign over Judah in the second year of Joash of Israel. The narrative turns south.

Arminian readers see a new king of Judah given his own opportunity to walk in the LORD’s ways.
verses.reformedNotes:
Both kingdoms have a king named Joash or Jehoash at this time, and the text distinguishes them by their fathers.

Reformed readers see God’s rule over both royal lines. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground and attend carefully to the similar names.

verses.text: He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign; and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jehoaddin of Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
Amaziah is twenty-five when he begins to reign, and he reigns twenty-nine years in Jerusalem; his mother is Jehoaddin of Jerusalem. The formula is standard for Judah’s kings.

Arminian readers see a long reign holding real possibilities.
verses.reformedNotes:
How these twenty-nine years fit with the reigns around them is debated, and some propose an overlap with his son’s reign.

Reformed readers see each reign set within God’s ordering of history. Both traditions read this as shared ground and hold such reconstructions tentatively.

verses.text: He did that which was right in the LORD’s eyes, yet not like David his father. He did according to all that Joash his father had done.
verses.arminianNotes:
Amaziah does what is right in the LORD’s eyes, yet not like David; he follows the pattern of his father Joash. The approval is qualified.

Arminian readers see genuine but incomplete devotion, a heart not yet wholly given to the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes:
David serves as the measure for Judah’s kings throughout Kings. Amaziah falls short of that standard.

Reformed readers see a reign that is commendable in part yet lacks wholehearted faithfulness. Both traditions read this as shared ground about mixed obedience.

verses.text: However the high places were not taken away. The people still sacrificed and burned incense in the high places.
verses.arminianNotes:
The high places are not removed, and the people still sacrifice and burn incense there. Reform remains partial.

Arminian readers see a king who leaves established practices in place rather than pursuing full obedience.
verses.reformedNotes:
The note about high places recurs for several otherwise approved kings of Judah, until Hezekiah removes them (2 Kings 18:4).

Reformed readers see worship still needing reformation according to God’s word. Both traditions read this as shared ground about incomplete reform.

verses.text: As soon as the kingdom was established in his hand, he killed his servants who had slain the king his father,
verses.arminianNotes:
Once his kingdom is secure, Amaziah kills the servants who had murdered his father. Justice follows consolidation.

Arminian readers see a king acting to punish a real crime once he has the authority to do so.
verses.reformedNotes:
The assassination of Joash of Judah is recorded in 2 Kings 12:20–21.

Reformed readers see the king exercising the sword against murder. Both traditions read this as shared ground and do not speculate beyond the text about Amaziah’s motives in delaying.

verses.text: but the children of the murderers he didn’t put to death, according to that which is written in the book of the law of Moses, as the LORD commanded, saying, “The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, nor the children be put to death for the fathers; but every man shall die for his own sin.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Amaziah spares the murderers’ children, following the law of Moses that each person dies for his own sin. The narrator commends his restraint.

Arminian readers see personal accountability before God’s law clearly affirmed.
verses.reformedNotes:
The quoted law corresponds to Deuteronomy 24:16. Amaziah applies it where vengeance on whole families might have been expected.

Reformed readers see God’s law restraining royal power. Both traditions read this as shared ground about justice and individual responsibility.

verses.text: He killed ten thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt, and took Sela by war, and called its name Joktheel, to this day.
verses.arminianNotes:
Amaziah kills ten thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt, takes Sela, and renames it Joktheel. His campaign succeeds.

Arminian readers see a genuine victory that will soon test the king’s humility.
verses.reformedNotes:
Sela means ‘rock,’ and its location is debated; Petra and other sites in Edom have been proposed. 2 Chronicles 25 gives a fuller account.

Reformed readers see success that becomes an occasion for pride. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Then Amaziah sent messengers to Jehoash, the son of Jehoahaz son of Jehu, king of Israel, saying, “Come, let’s look one another in the face.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Amaziah sends messengers to Jehoash of Israel, saying, “Come, let’s look one another in the face.” The words likely amount to a challenge.

Arminian readers see a king choosing confrontation after his success.
verses.reformedNotes:
The text does not state Amaziah’s reasons. The parallel in 2 Chronicles 25 supplies more background, but Kings keeps the focus on his challenge.

Reformed readers see confidence turning toward presumption. Both traditions read this as shared ground and avoid assigning motives the text leaves unstated.

verses.text: Jehoash the king of Israel sent to Amaziah king of Judah, saying, “The thistle that was in Lebanon sent to the cedar that was in Lebanon, saying, ‘Give your daughter to my son as wife.’ Then a wild animal that was in Lebanon passed by, and trampled down the thistle.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoash answers with a parable: a thistle in Lebanon asks a cedar for its daughter in marriage, and a wild animal tramples the thistle. The fable mocks Amaziah’s ambition.

Arminian readers see a pointed warning against overreaching.
verses.reformedNotes:
The parable casts Judah as the thistle and Israel as the cedar. It is a rhetorical put-down in the narrative, not a prophetic oracle.

Reformed readers see pride exposed even by an ungodly king. Both traditions read this as shared ground and treat the parable as narrative.

verses.text: You have indeed struck Edom, and your heart has lifted you up. Enjoy the glory of it, and stay at home; for why should you meddle to your harm, that you fall, even you, and Judah with you?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoash says Amaziah’s heart is lifted up by striking Edom; he should enjoy his glory at home rather than meddle and fall, with Judah. The warning is plain.

Arminian readers see Amaziah given a real chance to turn back.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jehoash names pride as the root of the challenge. His words, though arrogant themselves, prove accurate.

Reformed readers see wisdom spoken through an unlikely voice. Both traditions read this as shared ground about pride going before a fall (compare Proverbs 16:18).

verses.text: But Amaziah would not listen. So Jehoash king of Israel went up; and he and Amaziah king of Judah looked one another in the face at Beth Shemesh, which belongs to Judah.
verses.arminianNotes:
Amaziah will not listen, so Jehoash goes up and they face each other at Beth Shemesh in Judah. The battle is fought on Judah’s own ground.

Arminian readers see a free refusal of warning leading to consequences.
verses.reformedNotes:
Beth Shemesh lay west of Jerusalem in Judah’s territory, so the clash comes close to home.

Reformed readers see stubbornness bringing its own judgment. Both traditions read this as shared ground and describe the confrontation as the narrative presents it.

verses.text: Judah was defeated by Israel; and each man fled to his tent.
verses.arminianNotes:
Judah is defeated by Israel, and each man flees to his tent. The outcome is swift and decisive.

Arminian readers see the warning of verse 10 coming true as a result of Amaziah’s choice.
verses.reformedNotes:
The brief report contrasts sharply with the confident challenge of verse 8.

Reformed readers see the humbling of pride. Both traditions read this as shared ground, treating the defeat as narrative about the cost of refusing counsel, without drawing more from the text than it states.

verses.text: Jehoash king of Israel took Amaziah king of Judah, the son of Jehoash the son of Ahaziah, at Beth Shemesh and came to Jerusalem, then broke down the wall of Jerusalem from the gate of Ephraim to the corner gate, four hundred cubits.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoash captures Amaziah at Beth Shemesh, comes to Jerusalem, and breaks down four hundred cubits of the wall from the gate of Ephraim to the corner gate. Jerusalem’s defenses are breached.

Arminian readers see grave consequences of the king’s pride.
verses.reformedNotes:
A cubit is about 18 inches or 46 centimeters, so the breach is roughly 600 feet.

Reformed readers see Judah humbled by its northern neighbor. Both traditions read this as shared ground about pride’s cost.

verses.text: He took all the gold and silver and all the vessels that were found in the LORD’s house and in the treasures of the king’s house, the hostages also, and returned to Samaria.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoash takes the gold, silver, and vessels in the LORD’s house and the king’s treasuries, along with hostages, and returns to Samaria. Judah is plundered.

Arminian readers see the loss extending even to the temple’s treasures.
verses.reformedNotes:
Temple and palace treasures are taken or paid away several times in Kings. Here they are plundered after defeat.

Reformed readers see the seriousness of a king’s folly for his people. Both traditions read this as shared ground and do not speculate on the hostages’ identity.
